result.topic_en: Euler applies his interpolated-curve equation to the case θ = π, n = 1/2, relating an integral Δ to π(1+2ω)tan ωπ, argues that the correction function Φ vanishes to order higher than one at ω = 0, and then begins Problem 4, finding a curve through points whose abscissae form an interrupted arithmetic progression.
result.transcription:
$\omega(nn-\omega\omega)\frac{((n+1)^2-\omega^2)((n+2)^2-\omega^2)}{2(2n+1)\cdot 3(2n+3)}$ [?] etc.
quae per superiora est $=\omega(nn-\omega\omega)\mathfrak{A}=\frac{2\omega(n+\omega)}{\Delta}$. Vocetur haec quantitas $=\Omega$, sitque $f:\Omega$ eiusmodi functio ipsius $\Omega$, quae euanescat si $\Omega=0$, eritque aequatio generalis pro omnibus curuis satisfacientibus:
$y=\Theta+f:\Omega=\Theta+f:\frac{2\omega(n+\omega)}{\Delta}$.
Ac iam sine ullo dubio certum est, in hac aequatione contineri aequationem $y=\sin.\omega\theta$, posito $x=\omega\theta$, quandoquidem haec aequatio conditionibus praescriptis satisfacit. Ex quo euenire prorsus posset, vt aequatio $y=\Theta$ ab ista: $y=\sin.\omega\theta$, esset diuersa; quod imprimis pendere potest a valoribus, litteris $\theta$ et $n$ tributis, ita vt aliis casibus aequatio inuenta $y=\Theta$ cum hac: $y=\sin.\omega\theta$, conueniat, aliis vero ab eadem discrepet.

Scholion 2.
§. 34. Accommodemus hanc ad casum, quo $\theta=\pi$ et $n=\frac{1}{2}$ atque $\Delta=2\int\frac{x^{\frac{1}{2}-\omega}dx}{(1-x)^{\frac{1}{2}+\omega}}$; et quoniam seriei inuentae summa est $=\frac{\pi}{2\omega}\,\mathrm{tang}.\omega\pi$, habebitur haec aequatio generalis:
$\frac{\Delta y}{2(1+2\omega)\omega}=\frac{\pi}{2\omega}\,\mathrm{tang}.\omega\pi+\frac{\Delta}{2(1+2\omega)\omega}f:\frac{\omega(1+2\omega)}{2\Delta}$, seu
$y=\frac{\pi(1+2\omega)}{\Delta}\,\mathrm{tang}.\omega\pi+f\frac{\omega(1+2\omega)}{2\Delta}$,
vbi functio adiecta in genere ita est comparata, vt casibus
$\omega=0,\ \omega=\pm\frac{1}{2},\ \omega=\pm\frac{3}{2},\ \omega=\pm\frac{5}{2}$, etc.
euanescat, cuiusmodi formulae sunt: $\sin.2\omega\pi$, $\omega\cos.\omega\pi$; item $\sin.2i\omega\pi$ et $\omega\cos.(2i-1)\omega\pi$, denotante $i$ numerum integrum quemcunque; vnde quotcunque huiusmodi formulas pro lubitu combinare licet. Huiusmodi ergo dabitur certa quaedam functio; quae sit $\Phi$, vt fiat $y=\sin.\omega\pi$, hincque
$\sin.\omega\pi=\frac{\pi(1+2\omega)}{\Delta}\,\mathrm{tang}.\omega\pi+\Phi$, seu
$\Delta=\frac{\pi(1+2\omega)\,\mathrm{tang}.\omega\pi}{\sin.\omega\pi-\Phi}=2\int\frac{z^{\frac{1}{2}-\omega}dz}{(1-z)^{\frac{1}{2}+\omega}}$.
Cum igitur casu $\omega=0$ functio $\Phi$ certe euanescat, erit vtique $\Delta=\pi$, quod indicio est, functionem $\Phi$ factorem continere $\omega^{\lambda}$, cuius exponens $\lambda$ sit vnitate maior, quia alioquin, sumto $\omega=0$, quantitas $\Phi$ prae $\sin.\omega\pi$ non euanesceret. Atque ob hanc rationem conclusiones praecedentis problematis secundi pro veris sunt habendae.

Problema 4.
§. 35. Inuenire eiusmodi aequationem pro linea curua, inter abscissam $x$ et applicatam $y$, vt abscissis, in arithmetica progressione interrupta progredientibus, datae conueniant applicatae, scilicet:
Si sit $x=n\theta,\ (1-n)\theta,\ (1+n)\theta,\ (2-n)\theta,\ (2+n)\theta,\ (3-n)\theta$, etc.
vt fiat $y=p,\quad q,\quad r,\quad s,\quad t,\quad u$, etc.

Solutio.
Ponamus in genere abscissam $x=\theta\omega$, et pro aequatione inter $x$ et $y$ statuamus hanc aequationem:
$\frac{y}{\omega}$ [?] $=\mathfrak{A}\frac{p}{n}-\mathfrak{B}\frac{q}{1-n}+\mathfrak{C}\frac{r}{1+n}-\mathfrak{D}\frac{s}{2-n}+\mathfrak{E}\frac{t}{2+n}-\mathfrak{F}\frac{u}{3-n}+$ etc.
atque
Aa 3

items.quote: Ac iam sine ullo dubio certum est, in hac aequatione contineri aequationem $y=\sin.\omega\theta$, posito $x=\omega\theta$, quandoquidem haec aequatio conditionibus praescriptis satisfacit.
items.english: And now it is certain beyond any doubt that this equation contains the equation y = sin ωθ, putting x = ωθ, since this equation satisfies the prescribed conditions.

items.quote: Cum igitur casu $\omega=0$ functio $\Phi$ certe euanescat, erit vtique $\Delta=\pi$, quod indicio est, functionem $\Phi$ factorem continere $\omega^{\lambda}$, cuius exponens $\lambda$ sit vnitate maior
items.english: Since therefore in the case ω = 0 the function Φ certainly vanishes, we shall indeed have Δ = π, which indicates that the function Φ contains a factor ω^λ whose exponent λ is greater than one.

items.quote: Atque ob hanc rationem conclusiones praecedentis problematis secundi pro veris sunt habendae.
items.english: And for this reason the conclusions of the preceding second problem are to be held as true.

items.quote: Inuenire eiusmodi aequationem pro linea curua, inter abscissam $x$ et applicatam $y$, vt abscissis, in arithmetica progressione interrupta progredientibus, datae conueniant applicatae
items.english: To find an equation of a curve, between abscissa x and ordinate y, such that, the abscissae proceeding in an interrupted arithmetic progression, given ordinates correspond to them.
